nameStory: Northern arrowwood gets its name from Native American and early colonial use of its straight, flexible stems for making arrow shafts. The wood is dense and resilient, perfect for crafting hunting arrows that could fly true to their target. The 'northern' part distinguishes it from its close cousin, southern arrowwood, though their ranges actually overlap quite a bit!
description: Northern arrowwood is a medium-sized shrub that typically grows 6-10 feet tall, though it can occasionally reach small tree size. It has a rounded, somewhat open growth habit with multiple stems arising from the base. The plant produces clusters of small white flowers in late spring, followed by blue-black berries that wildlife love. Its leaves turn attractive shades of yellow, orange, or red in fall, making it both ecologically valuable and ornamentally appealing.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Opposite leaves that are oval to egg-shaped with prominent, straight parallel veins running from the midrib to the leaf edge. The leaves feel smooth on top and have coarsely toothed margins that are quite sharp to the touch.

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Small creamy-white flowers arranged in flat-topped clusters (called cymes) that are 2-4 inches across. Each tiny flower has 5 petals and gives off a subtle, sweet fragrance when you get close.

idTips.label: Fruit/Seeds
idTips.description: Dark blue to blue-black berries about 1/4 inch across that hang in loose clusters. The berries have a somewhat flattened stone inside and taste quite bitter if you're brave enough to try one.

idTips.label: Bark
idTips.description: Smooth grayish-brown bark on younger stems that becomes slightly furrowed with age. The bark has a clean feel and doesn't flake or peel like some shrubs.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Multi-stemmed shrub with an upright but somewhat spreading form. Stems are notably straight and flexible - you can bend younger twigs quite far without breaking them.

habitat: You'll find northern arrowwood in moist to wet areas throughout New England, especially along stream banks, in swampy areas, and in rich, mesic woodlands where the soil stays consistently damp. It thrives in bottomlands and forest edges where it gets partial sun to light shade. Look for it growing alongside other moisture-loving shrubs like elderberry and spicebush.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge bright green and fresh-looking, followed by the showy white flower clusters in late May to early June. The flowers attract various small pollinators and have that subtle sweet scent.
seasonality.summer: Foliage is full and green, providing good wildlife cover. Green berries begin forming and gradually darken as they ripen through late summer.
seasonality.fall: Leaves turn beautiful shades of yellow, orange, and red, while the dark blue berries ripen and become a favorite food for birds. This is often the easiest time to spot the shrub due to its colorful display.
seasonality.winter: Bare stems show the smooth bark and opposite branching pattern. Some dried berry clusters may persist, and the buds are small and pointed, arranged oppositely along the stems.

funFact: The stems of arrowwood are so strong and straight that they were once considered the gold standard for arrow shafts - some old-timers say a well-made arrowwood shaft could be reused dozens of times without breaking, making it more valuable than the arrowhead itself!
confusionNotes: Northern arrowwood is easily confused with southern arrowwood, and botanists still debate whether they're truly separate species. The key difference is that northern arrowwood has smoother leaves and leaf stalks, while southern arrowwood has tiny star-shaped hairs (you'll need a hand lens to see them). Memory trick: 'Northern = smoother.'
contextualKnowledge: There's ongoing botanical confusion about whether northern arrowwood is truly a separate species from southern arrowwood or just a variety of it. Some botanists lump them together as Viburnum dentatum, while others keep them split. This naming uncertainty reflects how closely related and similar these plants are - nature doesn't always fit neatly into our classification boxes!
compareHints: Among the viburnums, northern arrowwood is distinguished by its combination of coarsely toothed leaves, smooth leaf surfaces, and preference for wet areas. Unlike mapleleaf viburnum which has distinctly lobed leaves, or hobblebush with its huge heart-shaped leaves, arrowwood has simple oval leaves with straight parallel veins. The blue-black berries also help separate it from viburnums like nannyberry that have different colored fruits.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Among New England's viburnums, hobblebush is easily distinguished by its large heart-shaped leaves and drooping, rooting branches - most other viburnums grow more upright.
Among New England's viburnums, mapleleaf viburnum is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves - all other viburnums have simple oval or toothed leaves.
Among New England viburnums, northern wild raisin's thick, leathery leaves with smooth edges make it distinctive.
Unlike other viburnums in New England, guelder-rose is the only one with distinctly three-lobed, maple-like leaves.
Among New England's viburnums, nannyberry stands out for its tree-like size and glossy leaves with fine teeth all around the edges.
Unlike hobblebush with its large heart-shaped leaves or mapleleaf viburnum with maple-like foliage, southern arrowwood has distinctly toothed, oval leaves with straight parallel veins.

Unlike our native viburnums, Japanese snowball produces those distinctive perfectly round, sterile flower clusters rather than the flat-topped fertile flower clusters of species like nannyberry or arrowwood.

Among New England's viburnums, linden viburnum is most easily distinguished by its heart-shaped leaves - most other viburnums have either lobed leaves (like mapleleaf viburnum), elongated leaves (like nannyberry), or toothed oval leaves (like the arrowwoods).
Wright viburnum differs from native viburnums like arrowwoods and wild raisins by its more pronounced leaf venation and the distinctive red-to-black berry color change.
Siebold's viburnum stands out from other viburnums by its distinctively large, deeply ribbed leaves with parallel veining - most other viburnums have smaller leaves or different vein patterns.
Among New England's viburnums, squashberry is unique for its three-lobed, maple-like leaves - most other viburnums have either simple oval leaves (like nannyberry) or more complex tooth patterns.
Among the arrowwoods, downy arrowwood is distinguished by its fuzzy leaf undersides and earlier bloom time compared to southern arrowwood, which has broader leaves and longer leaf stems.
Among New England's viburnums, blackhaw stands out for its particularly hard wood and oval berries - most other viburnums have round berries.

**[UNCERTAIN]** Unlike the more common mapleleaf viburnum with its maple-shaped leaves or the arrowwoods with their toothed oval leaves, veiny viburnum's leaves are distinguished primarily by their extraordinarily prominent venation rather than their overall shape.

Tea viburnum differs from other New England viburnums by its oval berries that turn from red to black, rather than the round berries that stay red, blue, or black found in species like guelder-rose or arrowwoods.
Unlike native New England viburnums such as hobblebush or arrowwoods, wayfaring-tree has distinctly wrinkled, velvety leaves rather than smooth ones.
Among New England viburnums, Korean spice viburnum stands out for its incredible fragrance and compact size.
Among the viburnums, southern wild raisin stands out for its completely smooth leaf edges - most other viburnums have toothed leaves.
Unlike native New England viburnums which are all deciduous, leatherleaf viburnum keeps its leaves year-round.
